# Education in Sweden
Sweden’s education system is structured with compulsory schooling from ages 6–7 to 15–16, encompassing a nine-year comprehensive school (grundskola) divided into lower, middle, and upper stages. Following compulsory education, students typically attend a three-year upper secondary school (gymnasieskola), which offers preparatory (theoretical) and vocational programmes. Mandatory subjects in compulsory school include Swedish, mathematics, English, sciences, social studies, religion, and arts, with language courses like Spanish, French, or German introduced from grade 6. Grading starts in grade 6 using an A-F scale, and nationwide tests in grades 3, 6, and 9 ensure consistent assessment. Upper secondary education offers various national programmes, with admission based on compulsory school grades; students also complete a diploma project as part of graduation requirements.
Higher education in Sweden aligns with the Bologna Process, offering bachelor’s (basic level), master’s (advanced level), and doctoral degrees (third cycle), granted by universities and university colleges. Language proficiency in Swedish and English is required, and admission may include the Swedish Scholastic Aptitude Test (SweSAT). Education is publicly funded for Swedish, EU/EEA, and Swiss citizens. Vocational education exists but is separate from the university system and does not confer traditional degrees. Since the 1990s, independent (free) schools (friskolor) have been publicly funded and allowed to operate alongside public schools, offering alternative pedagogies, international curricula, or religious profiles, though their profit-making practices and impact on inequality have sparked debate. Sweden has participated in international assessments like PISA and PIRLS, with performance around OECD averages but challenges linked to immigrant student integration and testing inconsistencies being noted.
